reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Tachdjian's Paediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: The classic distal arthrogryposis affecting predominantly the hands and feet, with camptodactyly (fixed finger flexion), ulnar deviation and overlapping fingers, and talipes equinovarus (clubfoot)
Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable expressivity, so an affected parent may show only subtle finger contractures
Caused by variants in genes encoding the fast-twitch skeletal muscle contractile apparatus, most often tropomyosin (TPM2) or troponin I (TNNI2), with MYBPC1 in some families
Intellect and life expectancy are typically normal, and there is no progressive muscle weakness once contractures are established
The hand posture is characteristic: a tightly clenched fist with the thumb held across the palm (cortical thumb) at birth
Early passive stretching, serial casting and splinting improve range of motion, with surgical release reserved for fixed deformities
Family examination and a three-generation pedigree are essential because the phenotype is often milder in relatives
reference.pathophysiology: Distal arthrogryposis type 1 arises from pathogenic variants in genes coding for components of the fast-twitch skeletal muscle sarcomere, including beta-tropomyosin, troponin I and myosin-binding protein C. These variants disturb the regulation of the actin-myosin interaction and calcium sensitivity of contraction, altering muscle tone and force generation in the developing foetus. Reduced or unbalanced foetal movement (akinesia) during a critical window of limb development permits periarticular connective tissue to become fibrotic and joints to fixate in flexion, producing the congenital contractures of the hands and feet without a primary bone or nerve lesion.
additionalDifferentials: Amyoplasia with more proximal and symmetrical limb involvement
Isolated idiopathic clubfoot or isolated camptodactyly
Ehlers-Danlos or other connective tissue disorders with joint contractures
additionalInvestigations: Detailed clinical and dysmorphology examination with photographic documentation of hand and foot posture
Molecular genetic testing (targeted panel or gene sequencing for TPM2, TNNI2, MYBPC1 and related genes)
Three-generation family pedigree and examination of parents for subtle contractures
Plain radiographs of hands, feet and spine to characterise skeletal deformity
Prenatal ultrasound in at-risk pregnancies looking for reduced foetal movement and fixed limb posture
Electromyography or muscle biopsy only when a myopathic or neurogenic alternative needs exclusion
redFlags: Feeding or respiratory difficulty in the neonate suggesting more widespread neuromuscular involvement
Progressive weakness, which would point away from a static distal arthrogryposis toward a myopathy
Facial involvement or micrognathia raising concern for a syndromic distal arthrogryposis
Scoliosis developing during growth and requiring orthopaedic surveillance
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally favourable, with normal intellect and lifespan; contractures are static and functional outcomes are good after physiotherapy and, where needed, orthopaedic surgery, though some residual deformity and reduced grip may persist.
pitfalls: Assuming sporadic occurrence and missing a mildly affected parent, leading to inaccurate recurrence counselling
Labelling the clubfoot as idiopathic and overlooking the associated hand contractures
Delaying passive stretching and splinting, allowing contractures to become fixed
Attributing the condition to a progressive muscle disease and initiating unnecessary investigation or treatment
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Begin early passive stretching, serial casting, and splinting to improve joint range of motion
Provide physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maximise hand and limb function
Reserve orthopaedic surgical release for fixed, function-limiting contractures
Manage talipes equinovarus with Ponseti casting and surgery where needed
Follow up function and development, recognising the normal intellect and lifespan and static, non-progressive contractures
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and examine parents for subtle contractures
